exact_claim: 13 Sep 1848, near Cavendish, Vermont; railroad construction foreman Phineas Gage, 25
Tamping iron: 3 ft 7 in long, 1 1/4 in diameter, 13 1/4 lb, pointed
notes: Smooth tamping iron, not a crowbar

exact_claim: A spark ignited the powder while he tamped
notes: 'the powder went off' is the safest wording

exact_claim: The iron entered below the left cheekbone, passed behind the left eye and exited through the top of the skull, landing ~80 ft away
He spoke within minutes and rode sitting up in an ox cart about 3/4 mile to his hotel
To Dr. Williams: 'Doctor, here is business enough for you.'
He kept the iron as his 'constant companion' for the rest of his life (after reclaiming it from Harvard's museum)
Friends said he was 'no longer Gage'; Harlow: 'fitful, irreverent… grossest profanity'
Many textbook/popular accounts exaggerate him into a violent, dishonest drifter
About seven years in Chile driving six-horse coaches between Valparaiso and Santiago
Macmillan argues he made a surprisingly good psychosocial adaptation, helped by the structure of his work
Portraits of Gage holding the iron identified in 2009 and 2010

exact_claim: Died 21 May 1860 of seizures in California, about 36
Skull exhumed (1867) and with the iron given to Harlow; both now at Harvard's Warren Anatomical Museum
Exhibited at Barnum's museum in New York with his iron
Lost his foreman job: contractors 'could not give him his place again'
